terms.latin: Atque ex eō tempore beātē vīxērunt.
terms.gloss: and from that time on they lived happily
evidence: Cic. Amic. 15: ut beātē vīxisse videar
terms.comment: A closing line of ours for a tale, built on Cicero’s beātē vīvere, “to live happily”. It is a description: we have found no set closing formula for a story in the authors we searched or in Traupman, Morgan–Owens, or Levi–Bini. The ancient tellers end on the event itself: Apuleius closes the tale of Cupid and Psyche with their wedding and the birth of a daughter, and Ovid has Baucis and Philemon grow old together in their cottage (see the examples).
Ovid’s word for Baucis and Philemon, who grew old together in the cottage where they had married: with ūnā a closing line for a tale (see the examples).

phrases.latin: Rēx igitur et rēgīna ūnā beātī cōnsenuērunt.
phrases.english: And so the king and queen lived happily ever after.

phrases.latin: sed pia Baucis anus parilīque aetāte Philēmōn illā sunt annīs jūnctī juvenālibus, illā cōnsenuēre casā
phrases.english: but good old Baucis and Philemon, of the same age, were married in that cottage in their young years, and in that cottage they grew old

phrases.latin: sīc rīte Psȳchē convenit in manum Cupīdinis et nāscitur illīs mātūrō partū fīlia, quam Voluptātem nōmināmus.
phrases.english: So Psyche was duly married to Cupid, and in due time a daughter was born to them, whom we call Pleasure.
